# Small-text raster control

Original source generated by `tools/small_text_raster_fixture.py`: regular and
bold Book Antiqua/Arial at 7, 10 and 14 pt, white text on a green table background.
No corpus content, external artwork or font files are bundled. The reference application
exported `native.pdf`; `reference.json` records source/PDF hashes.

All 12 application glyph regions matched a separate native canvas fillText
call with identical font, color, baseline, spacing and transform: zero differing
pixel channels. The comparison canvas had only the flat green background and
one native text call. Native reference PDF rasterization still differs, especially for tiny
white letters. This is evidence against accidental bold or duplicate application
painting; it is not proof of pixel equivalence with the reference application or a completed fix.

Source, edited and undone controls pass schema validation. Browser editing,
package preservation, exact undo and reopening pass. Private inspection scripts
and PNGs are retained as `work/small-text-*` in the task scratch directory.

## Outline isolation, 2026-09-27

At equal 288-DPI resolution, a private browser hook painted installed glyph
paths instead of calling `fillText`. All 12 white-ink coverage measurements
moved closer to the native reference. The largest absolute relative coverage
error decreased from 24.29% to 1.42%; this measures ink amount, not positional
or pixel equivalence. See `tools/measure-small-text-coverage.py` for the method.
The original #66 business card also visually improves in the contact-text
region using the same hook and remains one editable page. Both controls passed
no-edit package equality, insertion with unrelated parts preserved, exact undo,
and reopening. This is a diagnostic result, not a completed rendering fix.

Loading the native reference PDF's embedded subset into the browser produced an RGB-identical
#66 page to the installed-font baseline. This rules out that subset's omitted
`gasp` table as the explanation in this experiment. Direct path painting is the
next implementation direction to evaluate, with browser shaping/advances and
performance still to be preserved. The hook itself is deliberately not shipped:
it supports only the four diagnostic faces and lacks general shaping/spacing
handling. No font binary or extracted contours are committed.

### Performance gate: direct path candidate rejected

A follow-up replay retained browser-measured glyph origins and cached every path
before timing. Two independent Edge contexts measured median replay times of
9.30/9.76 ms for native text and 21.52/22.78 ms for paths (19 distinct text calls).
Preparation added 156/213 ms, excluding font loading/parsing. This focused probe
is not whole-document timing, but the repeated paint regression is sufficient
to reject this candidate under the no-performance-regression requirement.
No production renderer change was made; #66 remains partial.

`paint-calls.json` contains original-control text only. Reproduce with
`node tools/probe-text-outline-paint.mjs tests/fixtures/small-text-raster/paint-calls.json C:/Windows/Fonts OUTPUT_PREFIX PLAYGROUND_URL`.
The probe needs locally installed Book Antiqua and Arial regular/bold. It writes
private PNGs and timing JSON, not fonts or glyph outlines.

### Native Canvas/SVG routes, 2026-10-03

`tools/probe-small-text-native-routes.mjs OUTPUT_PREFIX` captures a fresh finished
paint of this source, validates its source/PDF hash bindings, and replays the
19 calls using ordinary Canvas, four compensated em sizes and four SVG
text-rendering modes. All nine replay images are byte-identical in the current
Chrome environment. These routes do not fix the coverage discrepancy.
The diagnostic uses installed CSS fonts without reading font programs or
granting Local Font Access.
The older saved call list contains repeated paints and different text; it must
not be substituted for this fresh capture in a current-source coverage claim.
